content: 1. Ion emerges. 2. Exposure refers to the state of being, or potentially being, in contact with something, such as an infectious agent or an intervention. 3. Homogeneity in respondent-driven sampling surveys describes the extent to which individuals in a population share similar or identical characteristics, such as condom use or HIV status. 4. A partner survey involves using one population to recruit another related population. For example, sex workers (SW) in a survey may be asked to refer their clients for participation. 5. A primary survey directly samples the target population. 6. A probe is a request made by the interviewer for additional information or a technique used during an interview to help a participant recall specific details. 7. Semi-structured interviews involve using an interview guide with themes or open-ended questions grouped by topic areas to conduct an in-depth, open-ended conversation with respondents. 8. Survey implementation and quality assurance are critical components of data collection. 9. Data analysis and use follow survey preparation and implementation. 10. A participant shared, I first got paid to have sex three years ago. A man at a bar offered me money. I didn’t feel good about it and said I’d never do it again. About a year later, my sister was in an accident, and we needed money for her medical bills. Selling sex was the fastest way to make money. 11. Another participant stated, My boyfriend and I do not use condoms. We have been together for two years and get tested for HIV together. We agreed to be monogamous. I don’t think he has sex with other men, but it’s possible. I am always the insertive partner, so my risk of HIV is less. 12. A transgender woman explained, I’m a woman. Some people say I’m trans, and others say I’m a trans woman. But look at me, I’m a woman. I’ve always been a woman. It’s just that I started out with male genitals. So how can I be a trans woman if I’ve always been a woman? It’s what I am now. 13. A person who injects drugs shared, I used to use clean needles, but one of the places I got them from closed. I don’t have a steady job and cannot afford transport to the other place. It takes too long to get there too. Sometimes I reuse my own needles. Sometimes I share with others. It depends on the situation. If I’m out at a party and I’m able to get heroin, I’ll use whatever equipment is there. I don’t carry that stuff around with me all the time. But if I’m at home by myself, that’s where I have my stash. I don’t want to share it with others. 14. Qualitative data collection methods commonly used in bio-behavioral surveys (BBS) include semi-structured interviews, focus groups, and ethnographic mapping. 15. Semi-structured interviews are conducted with a series of open-ended questions, allowing for two-way communication between the interviewer and participant. This method enables the interviewer to adapt the course of the interview based on the participant’s responses and ask follow-up questions for further elaboration. 16. Semi-structured interviews provide an opportunity for investigators to explore a topic deeply and understand the reasoning and motivations behind behaviors. 17. Key informants are often interviewed using semi-structured methods. These individuals possess critical information that can aid in designing the BBS. They may include members of the target population and those with whom the members associate. 18. Key informants can serve as allies in engaging with the target population and navigating local politics. 19. It is essential to include diverse key informants to capture a wide range of perspectives. For example, in a BBS among men who have sex with men (MSM), consider including MSM of different ages, neighborhoods, socioeconomic statuses, education levels, HIV statuses, marital statuses, sexual identities, or levels of disclosure about their sexual behaviors. 20. Many countries have multiple terms for different types of MSM. Ensure these typologies are represented among qualitative study participants. 21. Similarly, non-MSM key informants should include individuals from diverse venues or service providers. 22. Building trust among the population through key contacts and visiting venues frequented by the population is crucial for the success of formative assessments, BBS, and supplemental studies. 23. Focus groups are semi-structured group discussions typically conducted with 6–8 members of the target population under the guidance of a facilitator using an interview guide. 24. Focus groups are useful for quickly collecting multiple viewpoints, especially on topics that do not require sharing private information. 25. Key informant interviews tend to elicit more thoughtful and personal responses, while focus groups often generate public responses, group discussions, and debates. 26. Using semi-structured key informant interviews and focus groups together accelerates data collection and allows investigators to compare responses from both settings. 27. Focus groups enable participants to interact with each other, sparking ideas and confirming or contradicting information shared by others. They also collect data faster than individual interviews. 28. Separate focus groups may be needed for subgroups within a population to understand their unique perspectives. For example, brothel-based and street-based sex workers, younger and older MSM, or methamphetamine and heroin injectors may require separate focus groups. 29. Audio recording interviews and focus groups is recommended to ensure detailed and accurate data collection. It is often challenging for an interviewer to take notes and conduct an interview simultaneously, especially in open-ended discussions. 30. Ethical review committees typically require consent for audio recording interviews and focus groups, and such recordings are considered personal identifiable information requiring special security safeguards. 31. An interview guide for qualitative studies may focus on specific topics or cover a range of themes. The richest results are obtained when the interview is conducted in a conversational format rather than a strict question-and-answer structure. 32. Administering a qualitative interview requires flexibility and readiness to adapt the discussion based on respondents’ answers. Skilled staff in qualitative methods are essential for conducting these interviews. 33. When developing an interview guide, it is important to: Stay consistent with the goals of the qualitative survey. Limit the interview to no more than one hour to avoid participant fatigue. Establish trust with the participant before the interview begins. Use open-ended questions and avoid leading or judgmental questions. Include probes to request additional information on key questions. Use the same terminology as participants to ensure clarity and rapport. 34. Probing is a critical skill for interviewers, allowing them to ask for elaboration, definitions, comparisons, or context to gather more detailed information.
